title: Line Chart Basics
markdown:
### The Scenario
You are tracking monthly sales for a small online shop.

### The Task
- Use `plt.plot()` to create a line chart of `months` vs `sales`.
- Give the chart the title: `Monthly Sales Trend`.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

months =['Jan', 'Feb', 'Mar', 'Apr', 'May']
sales =[120, 135, 150, 170, 165]

# Create your line chart below



# Display the plot natively
plt.show()
validation_code:
ax = plt.gca()
assert len(ax.lines) == 1, 'We could not find exactly one line. Did you use plt.plot()?'
assert ax.get_title() == 'Monthly Sales Trend', 'Check your plot title! It must be exactly Monthly Sales Trend.'
hints: Start with a single line connecting the month labels to the sales values.
Use `plt.plot()` to draw the line, then set the chart title.
Try `plt.plot(months, sales)` followed by `plt.title('Monthly Sales Trend')`.

title: Label Your Axes
markdown:
### The Scenario
A blog team wants to visualize website visitors across the work week.

### The Task
- Use `plt.plot()` to create a line chart of `days` vs `visitors`.
- Set the x-axis label to `Day`.
- Set the y-axis label to `Visitors`.
- Give the chart the title: `Website Visitors`.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

days = ['Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu', 'Fri']
visitors =[120, 150, 170, 160, 180]

# Create your chart below



# Display the plot natively
plt.show()
validation_code:
ax = plt.gca()
assert len(ax.lines) == 1, 'We could not find a line chart. Did you use plt.plot()?'
assert ax.get_xlabel() == 'Day', 'Check your x-axis label! It must be exactly Day.'
assert ax.get_ylabel() == 'Visitors', 'Check your y-axis label! It must be exactly Visitors.'
assert ax.get_title() == 'Website Visitors', 'Check your plot title! It must be exactly Website Visitors.'
hints: After drawing the line, make the chart easier to read by labeling both axes.
Use `plt.plot()` for the line, then `plt.xlabel()` and `plt.ylabel()`.
Try `plt.plot(days, visitors)`, then `plt.xlabel('Day')`, `plt.ylabel('Visitors')`, and `plt.title('Website Visitors')`.

title: Style a Line Chart
markdown:
### The Scenario
A fitness coach is plotting a runner's heart rate over time.

### The Task
- Use `plt.plot()` to graph `minutes` vs `heart_rate`.
- Make the line color `green`.
- Use a dashed line style: `--`.
- Give the chart the title: `Heart Rate Over Time`.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

minutes = [0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25]
heart_rate =[78, 88, 96, 101, 99, 90]

# Create your styled line chart below



# Display the plot natively
plt.show()
validation_code:
import matplotlib.colors as mcolors
ax = plt.gca()
assert len(ax.lines) == 1, 'We could not find exactly one line. Did you use plt.plot()?'
line = ax.lines[0]
assert mcolors.to_rgba(line.get_color()) == mcolors.to_rgba('green'), 'Your line color should be green.'
assert line.get_linestyle() == '--', 'Your line should use a dashed linestyle.'
assert ax.get_title() == 'Heart Rate Over Time', 'Check your plot title! It must be exactly Heart Rate Over Time.'
hints: You already need a line chart, but this time you also need to style how the line looks.
Use `plt.plot()` and pass styling arguments like `color` and `linestyle`.
Try `plt.plot(minutes, heart_rate, color='green', linestyle='--')` and then `plt.title('Heart Rate Over Time')`.

title: Compare Two Lines
markdown:
### The Scenario
A store wants to compare sales for two products across four quarters.

### The Task
- Plot `product_a` and `product_b` against `quarters` on the same chart.
- Add labels so a legend can identify each line as `Product A` and `Product B`.
- Show the legend.
- Give the chart the title: `Product Comparison`.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

quarters = ['Q1', 'Q2', 'Q3', 'Q4']
product_a =[120, 140, 160, 180]
product_b =[100, 135, 155, 190]

# Create your comparison chart below



# Display the plot natively
plt.show()
validation_code:
ax = plt.gca()
assert len(ax.lines) == 2, 'We expected two lines on the chart.'
legend = ax.get_legend()
assert legend is not None, 'We could not find a legend. Did you call plt.legend()?'
labels = {text.get_text() for text in legend.get_texts()}
assert labels == {'Product A', 'Product B'}, 'Your legend labels must be Product A and Product B.'
assert ax.get_title() == 'Product Comparison', 'Check your plot title! It must be exactly Product Comparison.'
hints: Plot both products on the same axes so the trends can be compared directly.
Use `plt.plot()` twice, give each line a `label`, and then call `plt.legend()`.
Try `plt.plot(quarters, product_a, label='Product A')` and `plt.plot(quarters, product_b, label='Product B')`, then `plt.legend()` and `plt.title('Product Comparison')`.

title: Add Markers to a Line
markdown:
### The Scenario
A weather station is plotting temperature readings across a week.

### The Task
- Use `plt.plot()` to create a line chart of `days` vs `temperature`.
- Add circular markers with `marker='o'`.
- Give the chart the title: `Daily Temperature`.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

days = ['Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu', 'Fri', 'Sat', 'Sun']
temperature =[29, 30, 31, 30, 32, 33, 31]

# Create your marked line chart below



# Display the plot natively
plt.show()
validation_code:
ax = plt.gca()
assert len(ax.lines) == 1, 'We could not find a line chart. Did you use plt.plot()?'
line = ax.lines[0]
assert line.get_marker() == 'o', 'Your line should use circle markers.'
assert ax.get_title() == 'Daily Temperature', 'Check your plot title! It must be exactly Daily Temperature.'
hints: This is still a line chart, but now each data point should be visibly marked.
Use `plt.plot()` with the `marker` argument.
Try `plt.plot(days, temperature, marker='o')` followed by `plt.title('Daily Temperature')`.

title: Resize the Figure and Add a Grid
markdown:
### The Scenario
A project manager wants a clearer chart for team output by sprint.

### The Task
- Set the figure size to `(8, 4)`.
- Use `plt.plot()` to chart `sprints` vs `tasks_completed`.
- Turn the grid on.
- Give the chart the title: `Sprint Output`.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sprints = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
tasks_completed =[12, 18, 17, 22, 24]

# Create your chart below



# Display the plot natively
plt.show()
validation_code:
fig = plt.gcf()
ax = plt.gca()
width, height = fig.get_size_inches()
assert abs(width - 8) < 0.1 and abs(height - 4) < 0.1, 'Your figure size should be 8 by 4.'
assert len(ax.lines) == 1, 'We could not find a line chart. Did you use plt.plot()?'
assert any(line.get_visible() for line in ax.get_xgridlines() + ax.get_ygridlines()), 'We could not detect a visible grid. Did you call plt.grid(True)?'
assert ax.get_title() == 'Sprint Output', 'Check your plot title! It must be exactly Sprint Output.'
hints: Set up the figure size first, then draw the line and turn on the background grid.
Use `plt.figure(figsize=(...))`, `plt.plot()`, and `plt.grid(True)`.
Try `plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))`, then `plt.plot(sprints, tasks_completed)`, `plt.grid(True)`, and `plt.title('Sprint Output')`.

title: Control the Y-Axis Range
markdown:
### The Scenario
A team lead is plotting project completion percentages and wants the full 0 to 100 scale visible.

### The Task
- Use `plt.plot()` to chart `weeks` vs `completion`.
- Set the y-axis limits from `0` to `100`.
- Give the chart the title: `Project Completion`.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

weeks =[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
completion =[10, 22, 38, 55, 74, 88]

# Create your chart below



# Display the plot natively
plt.show()
validation_code:
ax = plt.gca()
assert len(ax.lines) == 1, 'We could not find a line chart. Did you use plt.plot()?'
ymin, ymax = ax.get_ylim()
assert abs(ymin - 0) < 0.1 and abs(ymax - 100) < 0.1, 'Your y-axis limits should be 0 to 100.'
assert ax.get_title() == 'Project Completion', 'Check your plot title! It must be exactly Project Completion.'
hints: Plot the completion trend, then force the y-axis to show the full 0 to 100 range.
Use `plt.plot()` and then set the limits with `plt.ylim()`.
Try `plt.plot(weeks, completion)`, then `plt.ylim(0, 100)` and `plt.title('Project Completion')`.
